﴿The Inevitable Reality [al-Haqqah].﴾ ﴿What is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what the Inevitable Reality is?﴾ ﴿Thamud and 'Ad denied the Striking Calamity.﴾ ﴿As for Thamud, they were destroyed by the Overwhelming Blast.﴾ ﴿As for 'Ad, they were destroyed by a furious, roaring wind.﴾ ﴿He subjected it against them for seven nights and eight days in succession, so you could see the people lying prostrate in it as if they were the trunks of hollow palm trees.﴾ [69:7] ﴿So do you see any remnant of them?﴾ [69:8] ﴿Pharaoh, those before him, and the overturned cities came with sin.﴾ [69:9] ﴿They disobeyed the messenger of their Lord, so He seized them with a severe seizing.﴾ [69:10] ﴿Indeed, when the water rose high, We carried you in the sailing ship.﴾ [69:11] ﴿That We might make it a reminder for you, and that an attentive ear might retain it.﴾ [69:12] ﴿So when the Trumpet is blown with one blast,﴾ [69:13] ﴿and the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with one crushing,﴾ [69:14] ﴿on that Day the Occurrence will occur,﴾ [69:15] ﴿and the sky will split open, for it will be frail that Day,﴾ [69:16] ﴿and the angels will be upon its sides, and eight of them will bear the Throne of your Lord above them that Day.﴾ [69:17] ﴿That Day you will be exposed; nothing of yours will be concealed.﴾ [69:18]

Al-Husum (الحُسُومُ): al-Farra' said: it is from ḥasama l-dā' (حَسَمَ الدَّاءَ), meaning he followed up the disease with cauterization (بِالمِكْواةِ) on it. The poet said:

"Then a time separated their gathering, a time in which years followed one another in succession (ḥusum)."

Al-Mubarrad said: ḥasamtu l-shay' means I separated the thing from other things, and from this comes al-ḥusam (the sword). The poet said:

"So He sent a barren, westerly wind, and it circled over them, and it became ḥusum (unrelenting)."

Al-Layth said: al-ḥusum means ill omen (al-shu'm). It is said: "These are the nights of ḥusum," meaning they cut off good from their people. He said this in al-Sihah.

Ṣar'ā (صَرْعى): dead, its singular is ṣarī'. It is said of a thing that has grown weak and is ready to fall. Ibn Shajarah said: it comes from their saying wahiya (وَهِيَ), meaning the waterskin when it has torn. Among their proverbs is the saying of the rajaz poet:

"Leave alone the one whose waterskin has torn, and whose water has been spilled in the desert."

Al-arjā' (الأرْجاءُ): the sides, its singular is raja, meaning the side of a wall, a well, or the like. It is from the roots with waw, which is why it appears in the dual. The poet said:

"As if you had never seen before me a captive, shackled, nor a man thrown down by the two rajawan."

Another poet said:

"So he is not thrown down by the two rajawan. Indeed I am one of the few today who could take my place."

Hā' (هاءَ) with the meaning of khudh (take): there are dialects of it that we mentioned in the commentary on al-Tashil. Al-Kisa'i and Ibn al-Sikkit said: the Arabs say to a man: hā' (هاءَ), and to two men or two women: hā'uma (هاؤُما), to a man: hā'um (هاؤُمُ), to a woman: hā'i with a kasrah hamza (هاءِ) with no ya', and to women: hā'un (هاؤُنَّ). It was said: the meaning of hā'um is "take," and from it is the report about usury: "except hand to hand" (هاءً وهاءً), meaning each one says to the other "take." It was also said: it means "come here." Al-Qutaybi claimed that the hamza is a substitute for the kaf, but this is weak, unless he meant that it occupies its place in the dialect of those who say hāk, hākumā, hākum, hākunna, in which case it is possible that it is an artificial substitution, because the kaf is not substituted for the hamza nor the hamza for the kaf. It was also said: hā'um is a word set for answering the caller at times of joy and enthusiasm. In a hadith: a Bedouin called out to him with a loud voice, and he (peace and blessings be upon him) replied to him: "Hā'um," with the force of his voice. Some claimed that it is compound in origin, the original being hā' ammū (هاءَ أمُّوا), and then it was shortened by ease of use and common usage. Some claimed that this mīm is the pronoun for a group of males.

Al-quṭūf (القُطُوفُ): the plural of qiṭf, which is what is picked from fruit and plucked.

Al-silsilah (السِّلْسِلَةُ): well known, it is links that enter one another lengthwise. Al-dhira' (الذِّراعُ) is feminine and well known. The poet said:

"I shoot at it while it is a single, complete shaft, and it is three cubits and a finger."

Ḥaḍḍa 'alā l-shay' (حَضَّ عَلى الشَّيْءِ): he urged him to do it with emphasis.

Al-ghislin (الغِسْلِينُ): the linguists said: it is what flows from wounds when they are washed.

Al-watin (الوَتِينُ): a vein to which the heart is attached; if it is cut, its owner dies. Al-Kalbi said: a vein between the ʿilbā' and the throat. The ʿilbā' is the sinew of the neck, and there are two ʿilbāʾs with the vein between them. It was also said: a thick vein that the slaughterer's blade hits. From this is the saying of al-Shammakh:

"When you carried me and loaded my saddle to ʿArabah, you flowed with the blood of the watin."

This surah is Meccan. Its connection to what precedes it: when He mentioned some of the conditions of the happy and the wretched, and said: ﴿Leave Me with those who deny this discourse﴾ [68:44], He mentioned the narrative of the Resurrection and what God the Exalted has prepared for the people of happiness and the people of wretchedness. He interwove between them some of the conditions of those who denied the messengers, such as 'Ad, Thamud, and Pharaoh, so that the disbelievers who were contemporaries of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) might be warned by their mention and by what befell them. The Arabs knew of the destruction of 'Ad, Thamud, and Pharaoh, so He related this to them.

﴿al-Haqqah﴾: what is meant by it is the Resurrection and the Raising, as Ibn ʿAbbas and others said, because it is due (ḥaqqat) for every doer of his deed. Ibn ʿAbbas and others also said: because it reveals the realities of things. It was said: it is so named because the matter becomes binding (yaḥiqqu) in it, so it is from the pattern of "a sleeping night" (laylun nā'im). Al-ḥāqqah is an active participle from ḥaqqa l-shay' (حَقَّ الشَّيْءُ), when a thing is established and its validity is not doubted. Al-Azhari said: ḥāqaqtuhu fa-ḥaqaqtuhu uḥuqquhu, meaning I contended with him and I prevailed over him. So the Resurrection is "the Inevitable" (al-ḥāqqah), because it establishes the truth against everyone who contends with the truth through falsehood in the religion of God, that is, every disputant whom it overcomes. It was said: al-ḥāqqah is a verbal noun like al-ʿāqibah and al-ʿāfiyah. Al-ḥāqqah is the subject (mubtada', the element of a nominal sentence that is the topic), (mā) is a second subject, and al-ḥāqqah is its predicate (khabar, the comment), and the sentence is the predicate of "al-ḥāqqah." The linking element is the repetition of the subject by its own wording, as in: "Zayd, what is Zayd?" (mā) is an interrogative not meant in its literal sense, but for magnification. The repetition of the subject is most often used as a link when it is intended to express magnification and awe.

﴿And what will make you know what the Inevitable Reality is?﴾: this is hyperbole in expressing awe, and the meaning is that in it there is something that has not been known or grasped by any description of its hard matters and the details of its attributes. (mā) is also an interrogative subject, and (adrāka) is the predicate, and the pronoun of nominative case in (adrāka) refers back to (mā). (mā) is the subject, al-ḥāqqah is the predicate, and the clause is in the accusative position as the object of adrāka, and "adrāka" is suspended (muʿallaqah). The original usage of darā is to be transitive with bi- (in), and it may be omitted rarely. When the hamzah of causation enters, it becomes transitive to one object directly and to the other through a preposition. So His saying: (p. 321) ﴿What is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ after adrāka is in the accusative position after the preposition is dropped. And "al-Qāri'ah" (the Striking) is one of the names of the Resurrection, because it strikes hearts with its shock. Al-Zamakhshari said: it strikes people with calamities and terrors, the sky with its splitting and cleaving, the earth and mountains with crushing and scattering, and the stars with extinction and dispersal. He placed the pronoun so as to indicate the meaning of striking in al-Haqqah, increasing the description of its severity. When He mentioned it and magnified it, He followed this with mention of those who denied it and what befell them because of their denial, as a reminder to the people of Mecca and a warning to them of the outcome of their denial. End quote.

The majority read (fa-uhlikū) in the fourth form, in the passive. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read (fa-halakū) in the active. Qatadah said: "bi-l-ṭāghiyah" means with the cry that went beyond the limit of every cry. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: because of the transgressing act they committed. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Zayd also said, and Abu ʿUbaydah said something similar: al-ṭāghiyah is a verbal noun like al-ʿāqibah, so it is as if He said: because of their transgression, and this is supported by ﴿Thamud denied through their transgression﴾ [91:11]. It was also said: al-ṭāghiyah is the one who hamstrung the she-camel, and the ta' in it is for emphasis, like a man who is a great reciter (rāwiyah). All of them were destroyed because they approved of his deed. It was also said: because of the transgressing group. Al-Tabari and others chose that al-ṭāghiyah is the cry, and what supports this is that the cause of destruction for Thamud is paralleled with the cause of destruction for ʿAd, which is His saying: ﴿with a furious wind﴾. The discussion of ﴿ṣarṣar﴾ was mentioned in Surat al-Qamar. ﴿ʿātiyah﴾: it rebelled against its keepers and so went out without measure, or it rebelled against ʿAd, so they could not shelter from it, or it was described as such metaphorically for the intensity of its violence. Taskhir (subjugation) is using a thing with power over it. So the meaning of ﴿He subjected it against them﴾ [69:7] is: He made it stand and continue. ﴿for seven nights﴾ [69:7]: it began over them at the dawn of Wednesday, eight days before the end of Shawwal, until the end of Wednesday, completing the month. ﴿ḥusūman﴾ [69:7]: Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah, Mujahid, Qatadah, and Abu ʿUbaydah said: in succession, without any interruption within them. Al-Khalil said: bad omen and misfortune. Ibn Zayd said: ﴿ḥusūman﴾ is the plural of ḥāsim, meaning those days cut them off by destruction, and from it comes ḥasm (cutting off) of diseases and the sword. Al-Zamakhshari said: if it is a verbal noun, then either it is in the accusative by a hidden verb, meaning "it cuts off with ḥusūm," in the sense of uprooting with complete eradication, or it is a description, like your saying: "a day of ḥusūm," or it is an object of purpose, meaning He subjected it against them for uprooting. Al-Suddi read ḥusūman with a fatḥah, as a circumstantial accusative from the wind, meaning He subjected it against them uprooting them. It was also said: they are the days of barrenness, which are the end of winter. Their names are: al-Ṣinn, al-Ṣinnabr, al-Wabr, al-Āmir, al-Mu'tamir, al-Mu'allil, and Muṭfi' al-Jamr. It was also said: Mukaffī al-Ṭaʿn.

"Then a time separated their gathering, a time in which years followed one another in succession (ḥusum)."

Al-Mubarrad said: ḥasamtu l-shay' means I separated the thing from other things, and from this comes al-ḥusam (the sword). The poet said:

"So He sent a barren, westerly wind, and it circled over them, and it became ḥusum (unrelenting)."

Al-Layth said: al-ḥusum means ill omen (al-shu'm). It is said: "These are the nights of ḥusum," meaning they cut off good from their people. He said this in al-Sihah.

Ṣar'ā (صَرْعى): dead, its singular is ṣarī'. It is said of a thing that has grown weak and is ready to fall. Ibn Shajarah said: it comes from their saying wahiya (وَهِيَ), meaning the waterskin when it has torn. Among their proverbs is the saying of the rajaz poet:

Al-arjā' (الأرْجاءُ): the sides, its singular is raja, meaning the side of a wall, a well, or the like. It is from the roots with waw, which is why it appears in the dual. The poet said:

"As if you had never seen before me a captive, shackled, nor a man thrown down by the two rajawan."

Another poet said:

"So he is not thrown down by the two rajawan. Indeed I am one of the few today who could take my place."

Al-quṭūf (القُطُوفُ): the plural of qiṭf, which is what is picked from fruit and plucked.

This surah is Meccan. ﴿al-Haqqah﴾: what is meant by it is the Resurrection and the Raising, as Ibn ʿAbbas and others said, because it is due (ḥaqqat) for every doer of his deed. Ibn ʿAbbas and others also said: because it reveals the realities of things. It was said: it is so named because the matter becomes binding (yaḥiqqu) in it, so it is from the pattern of "a sleeping night" (laylun nā'im). ﴿And what will make you know what the Inevitable Reality is?﴾: this is hyperbole in expressing awe, and the meaning is that in it there is something that has not been known or grasped by any description of its hard matters and the details of its attributes. He placed the pronoun so as to indicate the meaning of striking in al-Haqqah, increasing the description of its severity. ﴿And what will make you know what the Inevitable Reality is?﴾: this is hyperbole in expressing awe, and the meaning is that in it there is something that has not been known or grasped by any description of its hard matters and the details of its attributes. (mā) is also an interrogative subject, and (adrāka) is the predicate, and the pronoun of nominative case in (adrāka) refers back to (mā). (mā) is the subject, al-ḥāqqah is the predicate, and the clause is in the accusative position as the object of adrāka, and "adrāka" is suspended (muʿallaqah). The original usage of darā is to be transitive with bi- (in), and it may be omitted rarely. When the hamzah of causation enters, it becomes transitive to one object directly and to the other through a preposition. So His saying: (p. 321) ﴿What is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ after adrāka is in the accusative position after the preposition is dropped. And "al-Qāri'ah" (the Striking) is one of the names of the Resurrection, because it strikes hearts with its shock. Al-Zamakhshari said: it strikes people with calamities and terrors, the sky with its splitting and cleaving, the earth and mountains with crushing and scattering, and the stars with extinction and dispersal. He placed the pronoun so as to indicate the meaning of striking in al-Haqqah, increasing the description of its severity. When He mentioned it and magnified it, He followed this with mention of those who denied it and what befell them because of their denial, as a reminder to the people of Mecca and a warning to them of the outcome of their denial. End quote.

The majority read (fa-uhlikū) in the fourth form, in the passive. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read (fa-halakū) in the active. Qatadah said: "bi-l-ṭāghiyah" means with the cry that went beyond the limit of every cry. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: because of the transgressing act they committed. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Zayd also said, and Abu ʿUbaydah said something similar: al-ṭāghiyah is a verbal noun like al-ʿāqibah, so it is as if He said: because of their transgression, and this is supported by ﴿Thamud denied through their transgression﴾ [91:11]. It was also said: al-ṭāghiyah is the one who hamstrung the she-camel, and the ta' in it is for emphasis, like a man who is a great reciter (rāwiyah). All of them were destroyed because they approved of his deed. It was also said: because of the transgressing group. Al-Tabari and others chose that al-ṭāghiyah is the cry, and what supports this is that the cause of destruction for Thamud is paralleled with the cause of destruction for ʿAd, which is His saying: ﴿with a furious wind﴾. The discussion of ﴿ṣarṣar﴾ was mentioned in Surat al-Qamar. ﴿ʿātiyah﴾: it rebelled against its keepers and so went out without measure, or it rebelled against ʿAd, so they could not shelter from it, or it was described as such metaphorically for the intensity of its violence. Taskhir (subjugation) is using a thing with power over it. So the meaning of ﴿He subjected it against them﴾ [69:7] is: He made it stand and continue. ﴿for seven nights﴾ [69:7]: it began over them at the dawn of Wednesday, eight days before the end of Shawwal, until the end of Wednesday, completing the month. ﴿ḥusūman﴾ [69:7]: Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah, Mujahid, Qatadah, and Abu ʿUbaydah said: in succession, without any interruption within them. Al-Khalil said: bad omen and misfortune. Ibn Zayd said: ﴿ḥusūman﴾ is the plural of ḥāsim, meaning those days cut them off by destruction, and from it comes ḥasm (cutting off) of diseases and the sword. Al-Zamakhshari said: if it is a verbal noun, then either it is in the accusative by a hidden verb, meaning "it cuts off with ḥusūm," in the sense of uprooting with complete eradication, or it is a description, like your saying: "a day of ḥusūm," or it is an object of purpose, meaning He subjected it against them for uprooting. Al-Suddi read ḥusūman with a fatḥah, as a circumstantial accusative from the wind, meaning He subjected it against them uprooting them. It was also said: they are the days of barrenness, which are the end of winter. Their names are: al-Ṣinn, al-Ṣinnabr, al-Wabr, al-Āmir, al-Mu'tamir, al-Mu'allil, and Muṭfi' al-Jamr. It was also said: Mukaffī al-Ṭaʿn.

**Verse 7–15 (Abu Hayyan, *al-Bahr al-Muhit*)**

﴿So you see the people in it﴾, meaning: in the nights and days; or in their dwellings; or in the directions from which the wind blows. These are possibilities, and the first is the clearest because it is the closest and is explicitly stated. Abu Nuhayk read *a'juz* (أعجز), on the pattern *af'ul*, like *ḍab'* and *aḍ'ub* (ضبع وأضبع). Al-Akhfash reported that it was read: "*nakhīl khāwiya*" (﴿hollow palm trees﴾), meaning their trunks were emptied through decay and corruption. Ibn Shajara said: the wind would enter through their mouths and exit through their posteriors, carrying out what was in their bellies of the broth (ḥasw), so they became like hollow palm trees. Yahya ibn Sallam said: their bodies were emptied of their souls. Ibn Jurayj said: they were in torment for seven days, then on the eighth day they died, and the wind cast them into the sea. This is His saying: ﴿Do you see any remnant of them?﴾ Ibn al-Anbari said: ﴿*min bāqiya*﴾ means *min bāqin* (any remnant), and the *ha'* is for intensification (*mubālagha*). He also said: "any remaining group" (*min fi'a bāqiya*). It was said that *min bāqiya* means *min baqā'* (any survival), a verbal noun that comes on the pattern *fā'ila*, like *al-'āqiba*. Abu Raja', Talha, al-Jahdari, and al-Hasan read it this way, with a variant from al-Hasan. Asim in the transmission of Aban, and the two grammarians (al-Nahwiyyan), read: ﴿*wa man qibalahu*﴾ with a kasra on the *qāf* and a fatḥa on the *bā'*, meaning: his troops and the people of his obedience. You say: "Zayd is *qibalaka*," meaning: in the place that is near you. The usage of *qibalaka* became so common that it came to mean the same as "with you," "in your direction," and "what is close to you, from whatever direction it is to you." The remaining seven readers, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and al-Sulami read: ﴿*wa man qablahu*﴾, with *qabl* as a time adverb (*ẓarf zaman*, an adverb of time), meaning: the disbelieving nations who lived before him, such as the people of Noah. He has alluded to some of his story after this.

﴿And the overturned cities﴾: these are the towns of the people of Lot. Al-Hasan read here: "*wal-mu'tafika*" (والمؤتفكة) in the singular. ﴿with the sin﴾, meaning: with the sinful deed or sinful deeds. Mujahid said this. Or it means "with the error," in which case it is a verbal noun on the pattern *fā'ila*, like *al-'āqiba*. Al-Jurjani said this.

﴿So they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord﴾: (*rasūl*) is a collective noun, referring to whoever came to them from God, such as Moses and Lot, peace be upon them. It was said that Lot (peace be upon him) is meant, returning the pronoun to the closest previous mention, which is "the messenger of the overturned cities." Al-Kalbi said that Moses (peace be upon him) is meant, returning it to the earlier mention, which is the messenger of Pharaoh. It was also said that *rasūl* means *risāla* (a message). ﴿Overwhelming﴾, meaning: growing. Mujahid said: severe, meaning that it exceeded the other seizures, which were drowning and the overturning of cities.

﴿Indeed, when the water rose﴾, meaning: it increased and rose above the highest mountain in the world by fifteen cubits. Ibn Jubayr said: it overflowed the treasurers, just as the wind overflowed its treasurers. ﴿We carried you﴾, meaning: in the loins of your fathers. ﴿In the sailing ship﴾: it is the ship of Noah (peace be upon him). The word *jāriya* was frequently used for a ship, and from this is His saying: ﴿And among His signs are the ships sailing in the sea like mountains﴾ [al-Shura: 32]. The poet said:

*Ninety jāriyas (ships) in the belly of a single jāriya.*

Al-Mahdawi said: the meaning is "in the sailing ships," meaning that this is by way of favor, and those carried are the ones addressed.

﴿So that We might make it﴾, meaning: the ship of Noah (peace be upon him), ﴿a reminder for you﴾ of what befell his destroyed people and the survivors who were saved in it, as an admonition. Qatada said: the first of this community reached it. Ibn Jurayj said: its planks were on al-Judi. It was also said: "so that We might make that sentence in the ship of Noah (peace be upon him) an admonition for you, by which you remember the salvation of your fathers and the drowning of the deniers of Noah (peace be upon him)." ﴿And retain it﴾, meaning: preserve its story. (An ear) whose nature it is to retain admonitions. It is said: *wa'aytu* for what is preserved within the self, and *awʿaytu* for what is preserved outside the self, in receptacles (*awʿiya*). Qatada said: the "retaining ear" is the one that understood from God and benefited from what it heard of the Book of God. In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ali: "I have asked God, Most High, to make it your ear, O Ali." Ali, may God be pleased with him, said: "After that I did not hear anything and forget it." He read: *wa-taʿiyahā* with a kasra on the *ʿayn* and the *yāʾ* lightened, the common reading. Ibn Musarrif and Abu Amr, in the transmission of Harun and Kharija from him, and Qunbul with a variant from him, read it with the *yāʾ* sukūn. Hamza read it with the *ḥaraka* concealed (*ikhfāʾ*). The justification for the sukūn is an analogy to forms that are of the pattern *fiʿl* in nouns and verbs, such as *kibd* and *ʿilm*. But *taʿī* is not of the pattern *fiʿl*. Rather, it is the imperfect (*muḍāriʿ*) of *waʿā*, which became *fiʿl*, and its original waw was deleted. Ibn ʿIsma (Asim's transmission) and Hamza al-Azraq narrated: *wa-taʿiyyahā* with the *yāʾ* doubled. It was said that this is an error, and it should be interpreted as meaning clear articulation of the *yāʾ*, to avoid those who make it sukūn, not as the merging of one letter into another. This should not be treated as doubling in pausal form, then applying pause to connected speech, though some have gone that way. It was narrated from Hamza, and from Musa ibn Abd Allah al-Anasi: *wa-taʿiyahā* with the *yāʾ* sukūn. This may be an independent sentence, which is the apparent meaning, or it may be like the reading ﴿*min awsaṭi mā tuṭʿimūna ahālīkum*﴾ with the *yāʾ* sukūn. Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask:) why is it said ﴿an ear, retaining﴾ in the singular and indefinite? (I answer:) to indicate that those who retain are few among them; to rebuke people for the scarcity of those among them who retain; and to show that when a single ear retains and understands from God, Most High, it is the great majority in the sight of God, Most High, and that what lies beyond it does not matter, even if they fill everything between the two horizons. End of quote. In it there is exaggeration.

When God, Most High, mentioned what He did to the deniers of the messengers of the torment in this world, He mentioned the affair of the Hereafter, what befalls the people of happiness and the people of wretchedness in it, and He began by announcing the Day of Resurrection. He said: ﴿So when the Horn is blown with one blast﴾. This blast is the blast of terror. Ibn Abbas said: it is the first blast, by which the world is ruined. This is supported by His saying: ﴿and the earth and mountains are lifted﴾. Ibn al-Musayyib and Muqatil said: it is the last blast, and on this view the crushing (*dakk*) does not come after the blowing, since the waw does not indicate order. This was also narrated from Ibn Abbas. When it was one time, it was emphasized by saying "one" (*wāḥida*). The majority read: *nafkhatun wāḥida*, both with *ḍamma*, and the tā' was not attached to *nafakha* because the feminine of *nafkha* is metaphorical and a separator intervened. Ibn Atiyya said: since it is qualified, its raising is valid. End of quote. Had it not been qualified, it would still be valid, because *nafkha* is a verbal noun with a defined sense, and its adjective is not a restrictive adjective but an emphatic one. (Abu al-Sammal read both with *naṣb*, placing the prepositional phrase in the position of the subject.) The majority read: *wa-ḥumilat* with the *mīm* lightened. Ibn Abi Abla, Ibn Miqsam, al-A'mash, and Ibn Amir in the transmission of Yahya read it with the *mīm* doubled. The lightened reading means that the earth and mountains were carried by a violent wind, or by angels, or by power without any intermediary creature. The view of those who say it is the earthquake is far-fetched, because an earthquake involves no carrying, only agitation. The doubled reading is either for intensification, or the doubling is for transitivity, so that the earth and mountains could be the first object placed in the position of the subject, with the second object omitted, meaning: a wind that crushes them, or angels, or power. It is also possible that the second is placed in the position of the subject and the first omitted, and it is one of the three presumed options. The pronoun in ﴿so they are crushed﴾ is dual, even though a plural pronoun preceded it, because what is meant is the totality of the earth and the totality of the mountains, meaning: some of them strike others until they are pulverized, and return as He, Most High, said: ﴿a heap of sand poured out﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 14]. Crushing (*dakk*) involves separation of parts, as in His saying "scattered dust" (*habā'an*), while pounding (*daqq*) involves irregularity of parts. It was said: it is spread out and becomes a level earth in which you see no crookedness or elevation. This comes from the expression "a *ádakk* camel" and "a *dakkā'* she-camel" when they are weak, so that their humps do not rise and their backs and ribs are level. ﴿Then on that Day﴾ is conjoined to ﴿when the Horn is blown﴾, and it is in the accusative governed by ﴿occurred﴾, just as ﴿when﴾ is in the accusative governed by ﴿is blown﴾, according to what we have chosen and established, and for which we have argued that the governing element of ﴿when﴾ is the verb that immediately follows it, not the response clause, though this opposes the view of the majority. The tanwin on ﴿*yawmaʾidhin*﴾ is a substitute for the omitted clause, which in estimation is: "on the day when the Horn was blown and such and such happened." ﴿The Event﴾ is the Resurrection. It has been mentioned earlier, regarding ﴿When the Event occurs﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 1], that some said it is the Rock of Jerusalem.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 69, verses 16–18:**

﴿And the sky will be split open﴾, i.e., it will be torn apart and its parts will be separated from one another. So on that Day it is split. ﴿Frail﴾: weak, because it splits after having been strong. ﴿Are you the more difficult to create, or the sky?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27]. Or it means "broken open," as one says: "the waterskin has split" (انخرق). It has also been said that its splitting is due to the descent of the angels. God the Exalted says: ﴿And the Day the sky will be split open with clouds, and the angels will be sent down in a descent﴾ [al-Furqan: 25]. It has also been said: its splitting is due to the terror of the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And the angel will be upon its edges.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: upon its sides (حافّاتها) when it splits. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "its sides" refers to the sky. Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: upon the edges of the earth. The angels will descend to it and guard its extremities, even though it has not been mentioned recently. It is also related that God the Exalted commands the angels of the lowest heaven, and they stand in rows on the edges of the earth; then the angels of the second heaven, who line up around them; then the angels of each heaven, so that whenever any one of the jinn and mankind tries to flee, he finds the earth encircled by them.

(al-Malak): a generic noun (ism jins) by which the angels are meant. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the difference between your saying 'al-malak' and saying 'al-mala'ikah' (the angels)?" I answer: "al-malak is more general than al-mala'ikah. Do you not see that your saying 'there is no angel (ma min malak) except that he is present' is more general than your saying 'there are no angels (ma min mala'ikah)'?" End of quote. It does not appear that al-malak is more general than al-mala'ikah, because a singular noun prefixed with the definite article of generic reference (al-jinsiyyah) can at most mean the plural with the same article; that is why an exception (istithna') may be made from it, so at most it is like the plural with the article. As for his claim that it is more general, based on his saying "Do you not see," it is not proof of his claim, because "min malak" is an indefinite singular (nakirah mufradah) in a negative context, and the preposition "min" (used to express comprehensiveness) has entered upon it, so it includes every angel, and the plural falls under it because the singular exists within it. Thus the negation extends to each individual. This is unlike "min mala'ikah," where "min" has entered upon an indefinite plural, so it generalizes to every plural group of angels, and it does not follow that every single angel is negated. If you say, "There are no men in the house (ma fi al-dar min rijal)," it is permissible that there is one in it, because the negation applies only to a plural, and the negation of the plural does not necessarily imply the negation of the singular. "Al-malak" in the verse is not in a negative context into which "min" has entered, so it would be more general than a plural into which "min" has entered (p-324). Rather, it came in singular form because it is lighter; and because His saying ﴿upon its edges﴾ indicates plurality, since a single being, as one, cannot be upon its edges at one time but only at different times. What is meant, God knows best, is that the angels are upon its edges, not that one angel moves over its edges at different times.

Al-Zamakhshari said: he means that it splits, and it is the dwelling of the angels, so they spread out to its extremities and what is around its edges. End of quote. The pronoun in "above them" (فوقهم) refers to "al-malak," a plural pronoun according to meaning, since it is intended as a generic class; al-Zamakhshari said this too. It has also been said that it refers to the angels who bear the Throne, i.e., above their heads. It has also been said that it refers to all the worlds.

The apparent meaning is that the omitted specifier (تمييز) in His saying "eight" (ثمانية) is "angels" (أملاك), i.e., eight persons of the angels. From al-Dahhak: eight rows. From al-Hasan: God knows best how many they are; are they eight rows or eight persons? They mentioned descriptions of these eight that are mutually contradictory, which we pass over without mention.

﴿On that Day﴾, i.e., the Day when what has been mentioned occurs, ﴿you will be presented﴾, i.e., for reckoning. "You will be presented" is the answer (جواب) to His saying: ﴿When the Trumpet is blown﴾ [al-Haqqah: 13]. If the blast is the first, then this is permissible, because the time-frame (اليوم) is extended and so it is made a time-frame for the blowing, and the occurrence of the Event and all created beings follow it. If the blast is the second, then no extension is needed, because His saying "then on that Day" (فيومئذ) is conjoined with "when" (فإذا), and ﴿On that Day you will be presented﴾ is a substitute (بدل) for "then on that Day." What follows these time-expressions occurs on the Day of Resurrection. The address in "you will be presented" is to all the worlds that are to be reckoned.

From Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud): Musa will see on the Resurrection three presentations: in two of them there are excuses, questioning, and disputes; and a third in which the scrolls fly out for the right hand and the left.

The majority read ﴿will not be hidden﴾ with the feminine ta' (لا تخفى). 'Ali, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, al-A'mash, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Ibn Miqsam, from 'Asim and Ibn Sa'dan, read it with the ya' (لا يخفى): ﴿any hidden thing (خافية)﴾: a secret and a state that used to be hidden in the world.

The apparent meaning is that the omitted specifier (تمييز) in His saying "eight" (ثمانية) is "angels" (أملاك), i.e., eight persons of the angels. From al-Dahhak: eight rows. From al-Hasan: God knows best how many they are; are they eight rows or eight persons? They mentioned descriptions of these eight that are mutually contradictory, which we pass over without mention.

﴿On that Day﴾, i.e., the Day when what has been mentioned occurs, ﴿you will be presented﴾, i.e., for reckoning. "You will be presented" is the answer (جواب) to His saying: ﴿When the Trumpet is blown﴾ [al-Haqqah: 13]. If the blast is the first, then this is permissible, because the time-frame (اليوم) is extended and so it is made a time-frame for the blowing, and the occurrence of the Event and all created beings follow it. If the blast is the second, then no extension is needed, because His saying "then on that Day" (فيومئذ) is conjoined with "when" (فإذا), and ﴿On that Day you will be presented﴾ is a substitute (بدل) for "then on that Day." What follows these time-expressions occurs on the Day of Resurrection. The address in "you will be presented" is to all the worlds that are to be reckoned.

From Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud): Musa will see on the Resurrection three presentations: in two of them there are excuses, questioning, and disputes; and a third in which the scrolls fly out for the right hand and the left.

The majority read ﴿will not be hidden﴾ with the feminine ta' (لا تخفى). 'Ali, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, al-A'mash, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Ibn Miqsam, from 'Asim and Ibn Sa'dan, read it with the ya' (لا يخفى): ﴿any hidden thing (خافية)﴾: a secret and a state that used to be hidden in the world.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 69, verses 16–18:**

﴿And the sky will be split open﴾, i.e., it will be torn apart and its parts will be separated from one another. So on that Day it is split. ﴿Frail﴾: weak, because it splits after having been strong. ﴿Are you the more difficult to create, or the sky?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 27]. Or it means "broken open," as one says: "the waterskin has split" (انخرق). It has also been said that its splitting is due to the descent of the angels. God the Exalted says: ﴿And the Day the sky will be split open with clouds, and the angels will be sent down in a descent﴾ [al-Furqan: 25]. It has also been said: its splitting is due to the terror of the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And the angel will be upon its edges.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: upon its sides (حافّاتها) when it splits. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in "its sides" refers to the sky. Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: upon the edges of the earth. The angels will descend to it and guard its extremities, even though it has not been mentioned recently. It is also related that God the Exalted commands the angels of the lowest heaven, and they stand in rows on the edges of the earth; then the angels of the second heaven, who line up around them; then the angels of each heaven, so that whenever any one of the jinn and mankind tries to flee, he finds the earth encircled by them.

(al-Malak): a generic noun (ism jins) by which the angels are meant. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the difference between your saying 'al-malak' and saying 'al-mala'ikah' (the angels)?" I answer: "al-malak is more general than al-mala'ikah. Do you not see that your saying 'there is no angel (ma min malak) except that he is present' is more general than your saying 'there are no angels (ma min mala'ikah)'?" End of quote. It does not appear that al-malak is more general than al-mala'ikah, because a singular noun prefixed with the definite article of generic reference (al-jinsiyyah) can at most mean the plural with the same article; that is why an exception (istithna') may be made from it, so at most it is like the plural with the article. As for his claim that it is more general, based on his saying "Do you not see," it is not proof of his claim, because "min malak" is an indefinite singular (nakirah mufradah) in a negative context, and the preposition "min" (used to express comprehensiveness) has entered upon it, so it includes every angel, and the plural falls under it because the singular exists within it. Thus the negation extends to each individual. This is unlike "min mala'ikah," where "min" has entered upon an indefinite plural, so it generalizes to every plural group of angels, and it does not follow that every single angel is negated. If you say, "There are no men in the house (ma fi al-dar min rijal)," it is permissible that there is one in it, because the negation applies only to a plural, and the negation of the plural does not necessarily imply the negation of the singular. "Al-malak" in the verse is not in a negative context into which "min" has entered, so it would be more general than a plural into which "min" has entered (p-324). Rather, it came in singular form because it is lighter; and because His saying ﴿upon its edges﴾ indicates plurality, since a single being, as one, cannot be upon its edges at one time but only at different times. What is meant, God knows best, is that the angels are upon its edges, not that one angel moves over its edges at different times.

Al-Zamakhshari said: he means that it splits, and it is the dwelling of the angels, so they spread out to its extremities and what is around its edges. End of quote. The pronoun in "above them" (فوقهم) refers to "al-malak," a plural pronoun according to meaning, since it is intended as a generic class; al-Zamakhshari said this too. It has also been said that it refers to the angels who bear the Throne, i.e., above their heads. It has also been said that it refers to all the worlds.

From al-Hasan: God knows best how many they are; are they eight rows or eight persons? They mentioned descriptions of these eight that are mutually contradictory, which we pass over without mention.

﴿On that Day﴾, i.e., the Day when what has been mentioned occurs, ﴿you will be presented﴾, i.e., for reckoning. "You will be presented" is the answer (جواب) to His saying: ﴿When the Trumpet is blown﴾ [al-Haqqah: 13]. If the blast is the first, then this is permissible, because the time-frame (اليوم) is extended and so it is made a time-frame for the blowing, and the occurrence of the Event and all created beings follow it. If the blast is the second, then no extension is needed, because His saying "then on that Day" (فيومئذ) is conjoined with "when" (فإذا), and ﴿On that Day you will be presented﴾ is a substitute (بدل) for "then on that Day." What follows these time-expressions occurs on the Day of Resurrection. The address in "you will be presented" is to all the worlds that are to be reckoned.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 69, verses 19–37:

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand, he will say: "Here, read my record!"﴾ ﴿"Indeed, I was certain that I would encounter my reckoning."﴾ ﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾ ﴿in a lofty garden﴾ ﴿whose fruits are within reach.﴾ ﴿"Eat and drink with satisfaction for what you put forth in the days past."﴾ ﴿But as for him who is given his record in his left hand, he will say: "Oh, I wish I had not been given my record"﴾ ﴿"and had not known what my reckoning is!"﴾ ﴿"Oh, I wish it had been the decisive end!"﴾ ﴿"My wealth has not availed me"﴾ ﴿"my authority has perished from me."﴾ ﴿"Seize him and shackle him,"﴾ ﴿"then burn him in the Blazing Fire,"﴾ ﴿"then bind him in a chain whose length is seventy cubits, so insert him."﴾ ﴿Indeed, he did not believe in Allah, the Mighty,﴾ ﴿and did not urge the feeding of the poor.﴾ ﴿So there will not be for him today any close friend here,﴾ ﴿nor any food except from pus,﴾ ﴿which none will eat except the sinners.﴾

"Amma" (ʾamma) is a particle of differentiation (ḥarf tafṣīl), by which what occurs on the Day of Presentation is distinguished. It appears that whoever among the monotheists is destined to enter the Fire will, on the Day of Presentation, take his record in his right hand together with those who are saved from the Fire, and this will be a comfort to him during the duration of the punishment. It has also been said: he will not take it until he has come out of the Fire, and his faith will be his companion during the duration of the punishment. It has been said: this is what appears [to be correct], because one who is being led to the Fire, how could he say: ﴿Here, read my record!﴾? Is this not rather an expression of joy and happiness? So it is not fitting for entry into the Fire. As for hāʾumu: if its meaning is "take," then it governs "kitābiyah" directly without an intermediary; and if its meaning is "come here," then it reaches it through the intermediary of "ilā." "Kitābiyah" is sought by hāʾumu and iqraʾū. The Basrans make "iqraʾū" operative, while the Kufans make "hāʾumu" operative, and in this is evidence for the permissibility of dispute (tanāzuʿ) between the ism al-fiʿl (the name-of-verb form) and the qasam (oath).

The majority read "kitābiyah" and "ḥisābiyah" in their places, and "māliyah" and "sulṭāniyah," and in al-Qāriʿah "māhiyah," with the retention of the hāʾ al-sakt (the silent hāʾ, a hāʾ pronounced at pause) both in pause and in continuity, in observance of the orthography of the Mushaf. Ibn Muḥayṣin read it with its omission both in continuity and in pause, and with the yāʾ made quiescent: "kitābī," "ḥisābī," "mālī," "sulṭānī." This was not transmitted in what I have checked in "māhiyah" in al-Qāriʿah. Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Aʿmash read with the hāʾ dropped in both, in continuity but not in pause, and Ḥamzah dropped them in "mālī" and "sulṭānī," and "mā hiya" in continuity but not in pause, and he opened the yāʾ in them. What al-Zahrāwī said, that the retention of the hāʾ in continuity is a grammatical error (laḥn) not permitted according to anyone I know, is not as he said. Rather, this is transmitted by mass transmission (tawātur), so it is obligatory to accept it.

﴿Indeed, I was certain﴾: that is, I was certain. Had it been a conjecture (ẓann) containing possibility, it would have been disbelief.

﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾: that is, one of satisfaction. Abu ʿUbayda and al-Farrāʾ said: "pleasing" means "pleased with," like His saying: ﴿from a gushing water﴾ [al-Ṭāriq: 6], meaning "gushed forth."

﴿in a lofty garden﴾: that is, lofty in place and in rank.

﴿whose fruits﴾: that is, what is picked from it. ﴿are within reach﴾: that is, close at hand; standing, sitting, and reclining persons can reach it with their mouths from its tree.

"Eat and drink": that is, it is said [to them]. As for "hanīʾan" (with satisfaction), its discussion has already preceded at the beginning of al-Nisāʾ. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Hanīʾan" means eating and drinking, pleasant (hanīʾan), or "you have been satisfied with satisfaction" as a verbal noun. End. His saying "eating and drinking, pleasant" appears to make "hanīʾan" an adjective of two verbal nouns, and this is not permissible except by an assumed elision according to those who permit that, i.e., "eating, pleasant, and drinking, pleasant."

﴿for what you put forth﴾: that is, what you sent ahead of righteous deeds. ﴿in the days past﴾: meaning the days of the world. Mujāhid, Ibn Jubayr, Wakīʿ, and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Rafīʿ said: they are the days of fasting, that is, in exchange for what you withheld from eating and drinking for the sake of Allah, Exalted. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿for what you put forth﴾ is general, that is, of righteous deeds.

﴿Oh, I wish I had not been given my record﴾: when he saw in it the abominable deeds he had done and what his matter would come to, he wished he had not been given it, and wished he had not known his reckoning, for his reckoning was revealed to him concerning what would grieve him in it, since it was against him and not for him. ﴿Oh, I wish it had been﴾: that is, the death I died in the world ﴿the decisive end﴾: that is, the one that cuts off my affair, so that I would not have been resurrected nor punished. Or: "Oh, I wish the state in which I now find myself had been the death I died in the world," since he saw that his present state is more bitter than the death he tasted. And how could it not be, when his affair has come to an everlasting punishment? ﴿My wealth has not availed me﴾: it is permissible for this to be a pure negation, which he reported lamenting his wealth because it did not benefit him; and it is permissible for it to be an interrogative which he used to reproach himself and to affirm against himself.

﴿My authority has perished from me﴾: that is, my proof, as said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿIkrimah, and al-Suddī. Ibn Zayd said: this is what the kings of the world say. ʿAḍud al-Dawlah Ibn Buwayh, when he named himself "King of Kings, Conqueror of Destiny," did not prosper and went mad; his tongue would not move except with his saying: ﴿My authority has perished from me.﴾

﴿Seize him﴾: that is, it is said to the guards (al-zabāniyah): ﴿Seize him and shackle him﴾: that is, put a shackle on his neck. ﴿then burn him in the Blazing Fire﴾. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Then you shall not burn him except in the Blazing Fire, which is the great fire, because he was a sultan who magnified himself over people." It is said: "ṣalā al-nār" and "ṣallāhu al-nār." End. He estimated it as "you shall not burn him except in the Blazing Fire" because he claims that fronting the object indicates restriction. We have discussed this with him at His saying ﴿You alone we worship﴾ [al-Fātiḥah: 5]. What he said is not the doctrine of Sībawayh nor of the expert grammarians. As for his saying "because he was a sultan who magnified himself over people," this is the saying of Ibn Zayd, and it is weaker; the preponderant view is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbās and those mentioned with him: that the sultan here is the proof he used to argue with in the world, because the one whose record is given in his left hand is not specific to kings, but is general to all the people of wretchedness.

﴿Then bind him in a chain﴾: that is, its measure and the magnitude of its length ﴿whose length is seventy cubits﴾. It is permissible for its apparent numerical meaning to be intended, and it is permissible for hyperbole to be intended concerning its length, even if it does not reach this number. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jurayj, and Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir said: by the cubit of the angel. Nawf al-Bakālī and others said: the cubit is seventy spans (bāʿ), in each span as the distance between Mecca and Kufa; this requires a sound transmission. Al-Ḥasan said: Allah knows by which cubit it is. It has been said: by the known cubit, and He addressed us only with what we know and can grasp. Ibn ʿAbbās said: if a link of it were placed on a mountain, it would melt like lead.

﴿So insert him﴾: that is, make him enter, like His saying: ﴿so He made it pass through springs﴾ [al-Zumar: 21]. The apparent meaning is that he is made to enter the chain, and because of its length it coils around him from all directions, so he remains within it, compressed, until it envelops him. It has been said: there is inversion (qalb) in the speech, and the chain enters his mouth and comes out from his anus, so it is in reality that through which he is passed. There is no necessity to take the speech away from its apparent meaning unless a sound proof indicates otherwise. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the meaning of fronting the chain before the passing is like its fronting the Blazing Fire before the burning: that is, you shall not pass him except into this chain, as if it were more dreadful than the other places of torment in the Blazing Fire. The meaning of "thumma" (then) is to indicate a difference between the shackling and the burning in the Blazing Fire, and between these and the passing into the chain, not a lapse of time. End. It has already been mentioned that his doctrine is restriction through fronting the object; as for "thumma," it is possible to keep it upon its original meaning of temporal interval, so that he is first seized and shackled, then when he is not punished quickly, he gets a rest, then the burning of the Blazing Fire comes, and that is more forceful in his punishment, since it comes to him when his soul has calmed a little. Then his passing comes after that, after being shackled and tormented in the Fire; yet he has a movement from place to place, so he finds some respite by it. When he is passed into the chain, that is the most severe punishment for him, since he has no movement and no transition, and it constricts him to the utmost. So in this case it is correct that "thumma" be upon its original meaning of temporal interval.

﴿Indeed, he did not believe﴾: he began with the strongest causes of his punishment, which is his disbelief in Allah. "Indeed" (innahu) is a resumptive causal clause, as if someone said: why is he punished with this severe punishment? It has been said: ﴿Indeed, he did not believe﴾ and the conjunction of ﴿and did not urge﴾ upon ﴿did not believe﴾ falls within the cause; and this indicates the enormity of the sin of one who does not urge the feeding of the poor, since he is placed as a companion of disbelief. This is the ruling for abandoning urging; how then would abandoning feeding be? The meaning is "upon feeding the food of the poor." He attributed the food to the poor because he did not attribute it to himself, since the poor has a right in the wealth of the affluent rich, even with the least abundance. The Arabs in their nobility and their preference (īthār) have wonderful and strange traditions, such that they are not found among others, and how fine is what has been said of them:

"Upon their wealthy is the provision of whoever visits them, and with the needy is generosity and giving."

Abu al-Dardāʾ used to urge his wife to increase provision for the sake of the poor, and he would say: "We removed half of the chain by faith; shall we not remove its other half?" It has been said: it is the prevention of the disbelievers. And their saying: ﴿Shall we feed him whom, if Allah willed, He would have fed?﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 47] means that when urging is negated, feeding is negated by way of priority, as He stated explicitly in His saying, Exalted: ﴿"We were not of those who prayed, nor did we feed the poor"﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 43–44].

﴿So there will not be for him today here any close friend﴾: that is, a tender, loving friend. ﴿Close friends on that day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67]. It has been said: a relative who would repel [punishment] from him.

﴿Nor any food except from pus﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās said: it is the discharge of the people of the Fire. Qatādah and Ibn Zayd said: it and the zaqqūm are the most evil and most hideous things. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Rabīʿ said: it is a tree which the people of the Fire eat. It has been said: it is something that flows from the people of the Fire; this is indicated by His saying in al-Ghāshiyah: ﴿They will have no food except from ḍarīʿ﴾ [al-Ghāshiyah: 6]. So they are one thing, or they overlap. It has been said: it is permissible for them to be different, and He informed about each one of them concerning a group other than the group whose food is the other. The predicate of "laysa" is "lahu" (for him). Al-Mahdawī said: it is not valid that "hāhunā" (here) be the predicate, and he did not clarify what prevents that. Al-Qurṭubī followed him in this and said: because the meaning becomes "there is no food here except from pus," and this is not valid, since there is other food there. "Hāhunā" is related to what is in "lahu" of the meaning of a verb. End. If there is other food than it there, and the eating is different from another eating, the restriction is valid in relation to the difference of the two eatings. As for if ḍarīʿ is ghislīn, as some of them said, then there is no contradiction, since what is restricted in the two verses is one thing; and that is prevented only from a direction other than what he mentioned, namely: if we make the predicate "hāhunā," then "lahu" and "al-yawm" would be related to what the predicate is related to, namely the operating element in "hāhunā," which is a notional operator, so its operand does not precede it. If the operator were verbal, it would be permissible, like His saying: ﴿And there is not for Him any equal, anyone﴾ [al-Ikhlāṣ: 4], where "lahu" is related to "kufuwan," and it is the predicate of "yakun."

The majority read "al-khāṭiʾūn" (the sinners) with a hamzah, an active participle of khaṭiʾa, which is one who does the opposite of what is right deliberately; and the mukhṭiʾ is one who does it without intention. Al-Ḥasan, al-Zuhrī, al-ʿAtakī, and Ṭalḥah, in transmission, read it with a dammah-vowelled yāʾ instead of the hamzah. Abū Jaʿfar, Shaybah, Ṭalḥah, and Nāfiʿ, in a variant from him, read it with a ḍammah on the ṭāʾ without hamzah; the apparent meaning is then an active participle of khaṭiʾa, as in the reading of the one who used the hamzah. Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is permissible that what is intended be: those who step over the truth into falsehood and transgress the limits of Allah. End. Then it would be an active participle from khaṭā yakhṭū, like His saying, Exalted: ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ [al-Nūr: 21], ﴿And whoever follows the steps of Satan﴾ [al-Nūr: 21], meaning he stepped toward sins.

His saying "eating and drinking, pleasant" appears to make "hanīʾan" an adjective of two verbal nouns, and this is not permissible except by an assumed elision according to those who permit that, i.e., "eating, pleasant, and drinking, pleasant."

﴿for what you put forth﴾: that is, what you sent ahead of righteous deeds. ﴿in the days past﴾: meaning the days of the world. Mujāhid, Ibn Jubayr, Wakīʿ, and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Rafīʿ said: they are the days of fasting, that is, in exchange for what you withheld from eating and drinking for the sake of Allah, Exalted. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿for what you put forth﴾ is general, that is, of righteous deeds.

﴿Oh, I wish I had not been given my record﴾: when he saw in it the abominable deeds he had done and what his matter would come to, he wished he had not been given it, and wished he had not known his reckoning, for his reckoning was revealed to him concerning what would grieve him in it, since it was against him and not for him. ﴿Oh, I wish it had been﴾: that is, the death I died in the world ﴿the decisive end﴾: that is, the one that cuts off my affair, so that I would not have been resurrected nor punished. Or: "Oh, I wish the state in which I now find myself had been the death I died in the world," since he saw that his present state is more bitter than the death he tasted. And how could it not be, when his affair has come to an everlasting punishment? ﴿My wealth has not availed me﴾: it is permissible for this to be a pure negation, which he reported lamenting his wealth because it did not benefit him; and it is permissible for it to be an interrogative which he used to reproach himself and to affirm against himself.

﴿My authority has perished from me﴾: that is, my proof, as said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿIkrimah, and al-Suddī. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jurayj, and Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir said: by the cubit of the angel. Nawf al-Bakālī and others said: the cubit is seventy spans (bāʿ), in each span as the distance between Mecca and Kufa; this requires a sound transmission. Al-Ḥasan said: Allah knows by which cubit it is. It has been said: by the known cubit, and He addressed us only with what we know and can grasp. The apparent meaning is that he is made to enter the chain, and because of its length it coils around him from all directions, so he remains within it, compressed, until it envelops him. It has been said: there is inversion (qalb) in the speech, and the chain enters his mouth and comes out from his anus, so it is in reality that through which he is passed. There is no necessity to take the speech away from its apparent meaning unless a sound proof indicates otherwise. It has also been said: he will not take it until he has come out of the Fire, and his faith will be his companion during the duration of the punishment. It has been said: this is what appears [to be correct], because one who is being led to the Fire, how could he say: ﴿Here, read my record!﴾? Is this not rather an expression of joy and happiness? So it is not fitting for entry into the Fire. As for hāʾumu: if its meaning is "take," then it governs "kitābiyah" directly without an intermediary; and if its meaning is "come here," then it reaches it through the intermediary of "ilā." "Kitābiyah" is sought by hāʾumu and iqraʾū. The Basrans make "iqraʾū" operative, while the Kufans make "hāʾumu" operative, and in this is evidence for the permissibility of dispute (tanāzuʿ) between the ism al-fiʿl (the name-of-verb form) and the qasam (oath).

The majority read "kitābiyah" and "ḥisābiyah" in their places, and "māliyah" and "sulṭāniyah," and in al-Qāriʿah "māhiyah," with the retention of the hāʾ al-sakt (the silent hāʾ, a hāʾ pronounced at pause) both in pause and in continuity, in observance of the orthography of the Mushaf. Ibn Muḥayṣin read it with its omission both in continuity and in pause, and with the yāʾ made quiescent: "kitābī," "ḥisābī," "mālī," "sulṭānī." This was not transmitted in what I have checked in "māhiyah" in al-Qāriʿah. Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Aʿmash read with the hāʾ dropped in both, in continuity but not in pause, and Ḥamzah dropped them in "mālī" and "sulṭānī," and "mā hiya" in continuity but not in pause, and he opened the yāʾ in them. What al-Zahrāwī said, that the retention of the hāʾ in continuity is a grammatical error (laḥn) not permitted according to anyone I know, is not as he said. Rather, this is transmitted by mass transmission (tawātur), so it is obligatory to accept it.

﴿Indeed, I was certain﴾: that is, I was certain. Had it been a conjecture (ẓann) containing possibility, it would have been disbelief.

﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾: that is, one of satisfaction. Abu ʿUbayda and al-Farrāʾ said: "pleasing" means "pleased with," like His saying: ﴿from a gushing water﴾ [al-Ṭāriq: 6], meaning "gushed forth."

﴿in a lofty garden﴾: that is, lofty in place and in rank.

﴿whose fruits﴾: that is, what is picked from it. ﴿are within reach﴾: that is, close at hand; standing, sitting, and reclining persons can reach it with their mouths from its tree.

"Eat and drink": that is, it is said [to them]. As for "hanīʾan" (with satisfaction), its discussion has already preceded at the beginning of al-Nisāʾ. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Hanīʾan" means eating and drinking, pleasant (hanīʾan), or "you have been satisfied with satisfaction" as a verbal noun. End. His saying "eating and drinking, pleasant" appears to make "hanīʾan" an adjective of two verbal nouns, and this is not permissible except by an assumed elision according to those who permit that, i.e., "eating, pleasant, and drinking, pleasant."

﴿for what you put forth﴾: that is, what you sent ahead of righteous deeds. ﴿in the days past﴾: meaning the days of the world. Mujāhid, Ibn Jubayr, Wakīʿ, and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Rafīʿ said: they are the days of fasting, that is, in exchange for what you withheld from eating and drinking for the sake of Allah, Exalted. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿for what you put forth﴾ is general, that is, of righteous deeds.

﴿Oh, I wish I had not been given my record﴾: when he saw in it the abominable deeds he had done and what his matter would come to, he wished he had not been given it, and wished he had not known his reckoning, for his reckoning was revealed to him concerning what would grieve him in it, since it was against him and not for him. ﴿Oh, I wish it had been﴾: that is, the death I died in the world ﴿the decisive end﴾: that is, the one that cuts off my affair, so that I would not have been resurrected nor punished. Or: "Oh, I wish the state in which I now find myself had been the death I died in the world," since he saw that his present state is more bitter than the death he tasted. And how could it not be, when his affair has come to an everlasting punishment? ﴿My wealth has not availed me﴾: it is permissible for this to be a pure negation, which he reported lamenting his wealth because it did not benefit him; and it is permissible for it to be an interrogative which he used to reproach himself and to affirm against himself.

﴿My authority has perished from me﴾: that is, my proof, as said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿIkrimah, and al-Suddī. ﴿Seize him﴾: that is, it is said to the guards (al-zabāniyah): ﴿Seize him and shackle him﴾: that is, put a shackle on his neck. ﴿then burn him in the Blazing Fire﴾. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Then you shall not burn him except in the Blazing Fire, which is the great fire, because he was a sultan who magnified himself over people." It is said: "ṣalā al-nār" and "ṣallāhu al-nār." End. He estimated it as "you shall not burn him except in the Blazing Fire" because he claims that fronting the object indicates restriction. We have discussed this with him at His saying ﴿You alone we worship﴾ [al-Fātiḥah: 5]. What he said is not the doctrine of Sībawayh nor of the expert grammarians. As for his saying "because he was a sultan who magnified himself over people," this is the saying of Ibn Zayd, and it is weaker; the preponderant view is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbās and those mentioned with him: that the sultan here is the proof he used to argue with in the world, because the one whose record is given in his left hand is not specific to kings, but is general to all the people of wretchedness.

﴿Then bind him in a chain﴾: that is, its measure and the magnitude of its length ﴿whose length is seventy cubits﴾. It is permissible for its apparent numerical meaning to be intended, and it is permissible for hyperbole to be intended concerning its length, even if it does not reach this number. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jurayj, and Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir said: by the cubit of the angel. Nawf al-Bakālī and others said: the cubit is seventy spans (bāʿ), in each span as the distance between Mecca and Kufa; this requires a sound transmission. Al-Ḥasan said: Allah knows by which cubit it is. It has been said: by the known cubit, and He addressed us only with what we know and can grasp. Ibn ʿAbbās said: if a link of it were placed on a mountain, it would melt like lead.

﴿So insert him﴾: that is, make him enter, like His saying: ﴿so He made it pass through springs﴾ [al-Zumar: 21]. The apparent meaning is that he is made to enter the chain, and because of its length it coils around him from all directions, so he remains within it, compressed, until it envelops him. It has been said: there is inversion (qalb) in the speech, and the chain enters his mouth and comes out from his anus, so it is in reality that through which he is passed. There is no necessity to take the speech away from its apparent meaning unless a sound proof indicates otherwise. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the meaning of fronting the chain before the passing is like its fronting the Blazing Fire before the burning: that is, you shall not pass him except into this chain, as if it were more dreadful than the other places of torment in the Blazing Fire. It has already been mentioned that his doctrine is restriction through fronting the object; as for "thumma," it is possible to keep it upon its original meaning of temporal interval, so that he is first seized and shackled, then when he is not punished quickly, he gets a rest, then the burning of the Blazing Fire comes, and that is more forceful in his punishment, since it comes to him when his soul has calmed a little. Then his passing comes after that, after being shackled and tormented in the Fire; yet he has a movement from place to place, so he finds some respite by it. When he is passed into the chain, that is the most severe punishment for him, since he has no movement and no transition, and it constricts him to the utmost. So in this case it is correct that "thumma" be upon its original meaning of temporal interval.

﴿Indeed, he did not believe﴾: he began with the strongest causes of his punishment, which is his disbelief in Allah. "Indeed" (innahu) is a resumptive causal clause, as if someone said: why is he punished with this severe punishment? It has been said: ﴿Indeed, he did not believe﴾ and the conjunction of ﴿and did not urge﴾ upon ﴿did not believe﴾ falls within the cause; and this indicates the enormity of the sin of one who does not urge the feeding of the poor, since he is placed as a companion of disbelief. This is the ruling for abandoning urging; how then would abandoning feeding be? The meaning is "upon feeding the food of the poor." He attributed the food to the poor because he did not attribute it to himself, since the poor has a right in the wealth of the affluent rich, even with the least abundance. The Arabs in their nobility and their preference (īthār) have wonderful and strange traditions, such that they are not found among others, and how fine is what has been said of them:

"Upon their wealthy is the provision of whoever visits them, and with the needy is generosity and giving."

﴿So there will not be for him today here any close friend﴾: that is, a tender, loving friend. ﴿Close friends on that day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67]. It has been said: a relative who would repel [punishment] from him.

If there is other food than it there, and the eating is different from another eating, the restriction is valid in relation to the difference of the two eatings. The majority read "al-khāṭiʾūn" (the sinners) with a hamzah, an active participle of khaṭiʾa, which is one who does the opposite of what is right deliberately; and the mukhṭiʾ is one who does it without intention. Al-Ḥasan, al-Zuhrī, al-ʿAtakī, and Ṭalḥah, in transmission, read it with a dammah-vowelled yāʾ instead of the hamzah. Abū Jaʿfar, Shaybah, Ṭalḥah, and Nāfiʿ, in a variant from him, read it with a ḍammah on the ṭāʾ without hamzah; the apparent meaning is then an active participle of khaṭiʾa, as in the reading of the one who used the hamzah. Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is permissible that what is intended be: those who step over the truth into falsehood and transgress the limits of Allah. End. Then it would be an active participle from khaṭā yakhṭū, like His saying, Exalted: ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ [al-Nūr: 21], ﴿And whoever follows the steps of Satan﴾ [al-Nūr: 21], meaning he stepped toward sins.

Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Aʿmash read with the hāʾ dropped in both, in continuity but not in pause, and Ḥamzah dropped them in "mālī" and "sulṭānī," and "mā hiya" in continuity but not in pause, and he opened the yāʾ in them. Rather, this is transmitted by mass transmission (tawātur), so it is obligatory to accept it.

﴿Indeed, I was certain﴾: that is, I was certain. Had it been a conjecture (ẓann) containing possibility, it would have been disbelief.

﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾: that is, one of satisfaction. Abu ʿUbayda and al-Farrāʾ said: "pleasing" means "pleased with," like His saying: ﴿from a gushing water﴾ [al-Ṭāriq: 6], meaning "gushed forth."

﴿in a lofty garden﴾: that is, lofty in place and in rank.

﴿whose fruits﴾: that is, what is picked from it. ﴿are within reach﴾: that is, close at hand; standing, sitting, and reclining persons can reach it with their mouths from its tree.

﴿for what you put forth﴾: that is, what you sent ahead of righteous deeds. ﴿in the days past﴾: meaning the days of the world. This is the ruling for abandoning urging; how then would abandoning feeding be? The meaning is "upon feeding the food of the poor." He attributed the food to the poor because he did not attribute it to himself, since the poor has a right in the wealth of the affluent rich, even with the least abundance. The Arabs in their nobility and their preference (īthār) have wonderful and strange traditions, such that they are not found among others, and how fine is what has been said of them:

"Upon their wealthy is the provision of whoever visits them, and with the needy is generosity and giving."

Abu al-Dardāʾ used to urge his wife to increase provision for the sake of the poor, and he would say: "We removed half of the chain by faith; shall we not remove its other half?" It has been said: it is the prevention of the disbelievers. ﴿So there will not be for him today here any close friend﴾: that is, a tender, loving friend. ﴿Close friends on that day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67]. It has been said: a relative who would repel [punishment] from him.

It is said: "ṣalā al-nār" and "ṣallāhu al-nār." End. He estimated it as "you shall not burn him except in the Blazing Fire" because he claims that fronting the object indicates restriction. We have discussed this with him at His saying ﴿You alone we worship﴾ [al-Fātiḥah: 5]. What he said is not the doctrine of Sībawayh nor of the expert grammarians. As for his saying "because he was a sultan who magnified himself over people," this is the saying of Ibn Zayd, and it is weaker; the preponderant view is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbās and those mentioned with him: that the sultan here is the proof he used to argue with in the world, because the one whose record is given in his left hand is not specific to kings, but is general to all the people of wretchedness.

﴿Then bind him in a chain﴾: that is, its measure and the magnitude of its length ﴿whose length is seventy cubits﴾. It is permissible for its apparent numerical meaning to be intended, and it is permissible for hyperbole to be intended concerning its length, even if it does not reach this number. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jurayj, and Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir said: by the cubit of the angel. Nawf al-Bakālī and others said: the cubit is seventy spans (bāʿ), in each span as the distance between Mecca and Kufa; this requires a sound transmission. Al-Ḥasan said: Allah knows by which cubit it is. It has been said: by the known cubit, and He addressed us only with what we know and can grasp. Ibn ʿAbbās said: if a link of it were placed on a mountain, it would melt like lead.

﴿So insert him﴾: that is, make him enter, like His saying: ﴿so He made it pass through springs﴾ [al-Zumar: 21]. The apparent meaning is that he is made to enter the chain, and because of its length it coils around him from all directions, so he remains within it, compressed, until it envelops him. It has been said: there is inversion (qalb) in the speech, and the chain enters his mouth and comes out from his anus, so it is in reality that through which he is passed. There is no necessity to take the speech away from its apparent meaning unless a sound proof indicates otherwise. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the meaning of fronting the chain before the passing is like its fronting the Blazing Fire before the burning: that is, you shall not pass him except into this chain, as if it were more dreadful than the other places of torment in the Blazing Fire. When he is passed into the chain, that is the most severe punishment for him, since he has no movement and no transition, and it constricts him to the utmost. So in this case it is correct that "thumma" be upon its original meaning of temporal interval.

Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Aʿmash read with the hāʾ dropped in both, in continuity but not in pause, and Ḥamzah dropped them in "mālī" and "sulṭānī," and "mā hiya" in continuity but not in pause, and he opened the yāʾ in them. Rather, this is transmitted by mass transmission (tawātur), so it is obligatory to accept it.

﴿Indeed, I was certain﴾: that is, I was certain. Had it been a conjecture (ẓann) containing possibility, it would have been disbelief.

﴿in a lofty garden﴾: that is, lofty in place and in rank.

﴿whose fruits﴾: that is, what is picked from it. ﴿are within reach﴾: that is, close at hand; standing, sitting, and reclining persons can reach it with their mouths from its tree.

﴿for what you put forth﴾: that is, what you sent ahead of righteous deeds. ﴿in the days past﴾: meaning the days of the world. If there is other food than it there, and the eating is different from another eating, the restriction is valid in relation to the difference of the two eatings. Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is permissible that what is intended be: those who step over the truth into falsehood and transgress the limits of Allah. End. Rather, this is transmitted by mass transmission (tawātur), so it is obligatory to accept it.

﴿Indeed, I was certain﴾: that is, I was certain. Had it been a conjecture (ẓann) containing possibility, it would have been disbelief.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: if a link of it were placed on a mountain, it would melt like lead.

﴿So insert him﴾: that is, make him enter, like His saying: ﴿so He made it pass through springs﴾ [al-Zumar: 21]. The apparent meaning is that he is made to enter the chain, and because of its length it coils around him from all directions, so he remains within it, compressed, until it envelops him. It has been said: there is inversion (qalb) in the speech, and the chain enters his mouth and comes out from his anus, so it is in reality that through which he is passed. There is no necessity to take the speech away from its apparent meaning unless a sound proof indicates otherwise. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the meaning of fronting the chain before the passing is like its fronting the Blazing Fire before the burning: that is, you shall not pass him except into this chain, as if it were more dreadful than the other places of torment in the Blazing Fire. ﴿Indeed, he did not believe﴾: he began with the strongest causes of his punishment, which is his disbelief in Allah.
