﴿Oh, I wish I had not been given my record﴾: when he saw in it the abominable deeds he had done and what his matter would come to, he wished he had not been given it, and wished he had not known his reckoning, for his reckoning was revealed to him concerning what would grieve him in it, since it was against him and not for him. ﴿Oh, I wish it had been﴾: that is, the death I died in the world ﴿the decisive end﴾: that is, the one that cuts off my affair, so that I would not have been resurrected nor punished. Or: "Oh, I wish the state in which I now find myself had been the death I died in the world," since he saw that his present state is more bitter than the death he tasted. And how could it not be, when his affair has come to an everlasting punishment? ﴿My wealth has not availed me﴾: it is permissible for this to be a pure negation, which he reported lamenting his wealth because it did not benefit him; and it is permissible for it to be an interrogative which he used to reproach himself and to affirm against himself.

﴿My authority has perished from me﴾: that is, my proof, as said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿIkrimah, and al-Suddī. Ibn Zayd said: this is what the kings of the world say. ʿAḍud al-Dawlah Ibn Buwayh, when he named himself "King of Kings, Conqueror of Destiny," did not prosper and went mad; his tongue would not move except with his saying: ﴿My authority has perished from me.﴾

﴿Seize him﴾: that is, it is said to the guards (al-zabāniyah): ﴿Seize him and shackle him﴾: that is, put a shackle on his neck. ﴿then burn him in the Blazing Fire﴾. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Then you shall not burn him except in the Blazing Fire, which is the great fire, because he was a sultan who magnified himself over people." It is said: "ṣalā al-nār" and "ṣallāhu al-nār." End. He estimated it as "you shall not burn him except in the Blazing Fire" because he claims that fronting the object indicates restriction. We have discussed this with him at His saying ﴿You alone we worship﴾ [al-Fātiḥah: 5]. What he said is not the doctrine of Sībawayh nor of the expert grammarians. As for his saying "because he was a sultan who magnified himself over people," this is the saying of Ibn Zayd, and it is weaker; the preponderant view is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbās and those mentioned with him: that the sultan here is the proof he used to argue with in the world, because the one whose record is given in his left hand is not specific to kings, but is general to all the people of wretchedness.

﴿Then bind him in a chain﴾: that is, its measure and the magnitude of its length ﴿whose length is seventy cubits﴾. It is permissible for its apparent numerical meaning to be intended, and it is permissible for hyperbole to be intended concerning its length, even if it does not reach this number. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jurayj, and Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir said: by the cubit of the angel. Nawf al-Bakālī and others said: the cubit is seventy spans (bāʿ), in each span as the distance between Mecca and Kufa; this requires a sound transmission. Al-Ḥasan said: Allah knows by which cubit it is. It has been said: by the known cubit, and He addressed us only with what we know and can grasp. Ibn ʿAbbās said: if a link of it were placed on a mountain, it would melt like lead.

﴿So insert him﴾: that is, make him enter, like His saying: ﴿so He made it pass through springs﴾ [al-Zumar: 21]. The apparent meaning is that he is made to enter the chain, and because of its length it coils around him from all directions, so he remains within it, compressed, until it envelops him. It has been said: there is inversion (qalb) in the speech, and the chain enters his mouth and comes out from his anus, so it is in reality that through which he is passed. There is no necessity to take the speech away from its apparent meaning unless a sound proof indicates otherwise. Al-Zamakhsharī said: the meaning of fronting the chain before the passing is like its fronting the Blazing Fire before the burning: that is, you shall not pass him except into this chain, as if it were more dreadful than the other places of torment in the Blazing Fire. The meaning of "thumma" (then) is to indicate a difference between the shackling and the burning in the Blazing Fire, and between these and the passing into the chain, not a lapse of time. End. It has already been mentioned that his doctrine is restriction through fronting the object; as for "thumma," it is possible to keep it upon its original meaning of temporal interval, so that he is first seized and shackled, then when he is not punished quickly, he gets a rest, then the burning of the Blazing Fire comes, and that is more forceful in his punishment, since it comes to him when his soul has calmed a little. Then his passing comes after that, after being shackled and tormented in the Fire; yet he has a movement from place to place, so he finds some respite by it. When he is passed into the chain, that is the most severe punishment for him, since he has no movement and no transition, and it constricts him to the utmost. So in this case it is correct that "thumma" be upon its original meaning of temporal interval.

﴿Indeed, he did not believe﴾: he began with the strongest causes of his punishment, which is his disbelief in Allah. "Indeed" (innahu) is a resumptive causal clause, as if someone said: why is he punished with this severe punishment? It has been said: ﴿Indeed, he did not believe﴾ and the conjunction of ﴿and did not urge﴾ upon ﴿did not believe﴾ falls within the cause; and this indicates the enormity of the sin of one who does not urge the feeding of the poor, since he is placed as a companion of disbelief. This is the ruling for abandoning urging; how then would abandoning feeding be? The meaning is "upon feeding the food of the poor." He attributed the food to the poor because he did not attribute it to himself, since the poor has a right in the wealth of the affluent rich, even with the least abundance. ﴿So there will not be for him today here any close friend﴾: that is, a tender, loving friend. ﴿Close friends on that day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67]. It has been said: a relative who would repel [punishment] from him.

﴿Nor any food except from pus﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās said: it is the discharge of the people of the Fire. Qatādah and Ibn Zayd said: it and the zaqqūm are the most evil and most hideous things. "Hāhunā" is related to what is in "lahu" of the meaning of a verb. End. If there is other food than it there, and the eating is different from another eating, the restriction is valid in relation to the difference of the two eatings. Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is permissible that what is intended be: those who step over the truth into falsehood and transgress the limits of Allah. End. Then it would be an active participle from khaṭā yakhṭū, like His saying, Exalted: ﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ [al-Nūr: 21], ﴿And whoever follows the steps of Satan﴾ [al-Nūr: 21], meaning he stepped toward sins.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 69, verses 19–37:

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand, he will say: "Here, read my record!"﴾ ﴿"Indeed, I was certain that I would encounter my reckoning."﴾ ﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾ ﴿in a lofty garden﴾ ﴿whose fruits are within reach.﴾ ﴿"Eat and drink with satisfaction for what you put forth in the days past."﴾ ﴿But as for him who is given his record in his left hand, he will say: "Oh, I wish I had not been given my record"﴾ ﴿"and had not known what my reckoning is!"﴾ ﴿"Oh, I wish it had been the decisive end!"﴾ ﴿"My wealth has not availed me"﴾ ﴿"my authority has perished from me."﴾ ﴿"Seize him and shackle him,"﴾ ﴿"then burn him in the Blazing Fire,"﴾ ﴿"then bind him in a chain whose length is seventy cubits, so insert him."﴾ ﴿Indeed, he did not believe in Allah, the Mighty,﴾ ﴿and did not urge the feeding of the poor.﴾ ﴿So there will not be for him today any close friend here,﴾ ﴿nor any food except from pus,﴾ ﴿which none will eat except the sinners.﴾

"Amma" (ʾamma) is a particle of differentiation (ḥarf tafṣīl), by which what occurs on the Day of Presentation is distinguished. It appears that whoever among the monotheists is destined to enter the Fire will, on the Day of Presentation, take his record in his right hand together with those who are saved from the Fire, and this will be a comfort to him during the duration of the punishment. It has also been said: he will not take it until he has come out of the Fire, and his faith will be his companion during the duration of the punishment. It has been said: this is what appears [to be correct], because one who is being led to the Fire, how could he say: ﴿Here, read my record!﴾? Is this not rather an expression of joy and happiness? So it is not fitting for entry into the Fire. As for hāʾumu: if its meaning is "take," then it governs "kitābiyah" directly without an intermediary; and if its meaning is "come here," then it reaches it through the intermediary of "ilā." "Kitābiyah" is sought by hāʾumu and iqraʾū. The Basrans make "iqraʾū" operative, while the Kufans make "hāʾumu" operative, and in this is evidence for the permissibility of dispute (tanāzuʿ) between the ism al-fiʿl (the name-of-verb form) and the qasam (oath).

The majority read "kitābiyah" and "ḥisābiyah" in their places, and "māliyah" and "sulṭāniyah," and in al-Qāriʿah "māhiyah," with the retention of the hāʾ al-sakt (the silent hāʾ, a hāʾ pronounced at pause) both in pause and in continuity, in observance of the orthography of the Mushaf. Ibn Muḥayṣin read it with its omission both in continuity and in pause, and with the yāʾ made quiescent: "kitābī," "ḥisābī," "mālī," "sulṭānī." This was not transmitted in what I have checked in "māhiyah" in al-Qāriʿah. Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-Aʿmash read with the hāʾ dropped in both, in continuity but not in pause, and Ḥamzah dropped them in "mālī" and "sulṭānī," and "mā hiya" in continuity but not in pause, and he opened the yāʾ in them. What al-Zahrāwī said, that the retention of the hāʾ in continuity is a grammatical error (laḥn) not permitted according to anyone I know, is not as he said. Rather, this is transmitted by mass transmission (tawātur), so it is obligatory to accept it.

﴿Indeed, I was certain﴾: that is, I was certain. Had it been a conjecture (ẓann) containing possibility, it would have been disbelief.

﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾: that is, one of satisfaction. Abu ʿUbayda and al-Farrāʾ said: "pleasing" means "pleased with," like His saying: ﴿from a gushing water﴾ [al-Ṭāriq: 6], meaning "gushed forth."

﴿in a lofty garden﴾: that is, lofty in place and in rank.

﴿whose fruits﴾: that is, what is picked from it. ﴿are within reach﴾: that is, close at hand; standing, sitting, and reclining persons can reach it with their mouths from its tree.

"Eat and drink": that is, it is said [to them]. As for "hanīʾan" (with satisfaction), its discussion has already preceded at the beginning of al-Nisāʾ. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Hanīʾan" means eating and drinking, pleasant (hanīʾan), or "you have been satisfied with satisfaction" as a verbal noun. End. His saying "eating and drinking, pleasant" appears to make "hanīʾan" an adjective of two verbal nouns, and this is not permissible except by an assumed elision according to those who permit that, i.e., "eating, pleasant, and drinking, pleasant."

﴿for what you put forth﴾: that is, what you sent ahead of righteous deeds. ﴿in the days past﴾: meaning the days of the world. ﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ ﴿and what you do not see﴾ ﴿that it is indeed the word of a noble messenger﴾ ﴿and it is not the word of a poet—little do you believe﴾ ﴿nor the word of a soothsayer—little do you take heed﴾ ﴿it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿and if he had fabricated against Us some sayings﴾ ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ ﴿then We would have cut off his aorta﴾ ﴿and none of you could have held Us back from him﴾ ﴿and indeed it is a reminder for the God-fearing﴾ ﴿and indeed We know that among you are deniers﴾ ﴿and indeed it is a cause of regret for the disbelievers﴾ ﴿and indeed it is the sure truth﴾ ﴿so glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾.

[p. 328] The discussion of the particle *lā* (لا) before the oath has already been given at His words: ﴿So I swear by the places of the stars﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:75]. The recitation of al-Hasan (qira'ah, a canonical or variant reading) is *la-uqsimu bi-jaʿlihā* (لَأُقْسِمُ بِجَعْلِها), in which *lā* is not placed before *uqsimu*. It has also been said that *lā* here is a negation of the oath, meaning: there is no need for an oath in this matter because the truth in it is clear. On this view, its answer is the answer of the oath. Muqatil said: the reason for this is that al-Walid said, "Muhammad is a sorcerer," Abu Jahl said, "He is a poet," and another said, "He is a soothsayer." So God refuted them with His words: ﴿So I swear by what you see and what you do not see﴾, which is general over all His creation. ʿAtaʾ said: what you see are the traces of power, and what you do not see are the secrets of power. It has also been said: ﴿what you do not see﴾ refers to the angels. It has been said that it refers to bodies and spirits.

(*Innahu*) meaning: indeed the Qur'an ﴿is the word of a noble messenger﴾, namely Muhammad (ﷺ), according to the majority. This is supported by ﴿nor the word of a poet﴾ and what follows it. The saying is attributed to him because he is the one who conveys it and acts upon it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Smallness (*qillah*) is in the sense of non-existence, meaning: you do not believe and you do not take heed at all, and the meaning is: how disbelieving you are and how heedless you are." End of quotation. *Few are the voices in it except its bellowing.*

God negated that it is the word of a poet because it differs from the various forms of poetry, nor the word of a soothsayer because it was revealed without the agency of the devils. *Qalīlan* (قَلِيلًا) is in the accusative as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun or an omitted time expression, meaning: you believe a little belief, or for a little time. The same applies to ﴿little do you take heed﴾. The "little" is their acknowledgment when they are asked who created them, and they say: "God." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: *qalīlan* is governed by a hidden verb indicated by *tu'minūn* (you believe), and *mā* may be negative, so that their faith is entirely negated; or *mā* may be a verbal particle (maṣdariyyah), and what is characterised by smallness is the linguistic faith, because they affirmed certain small matters that did not benefit them at all, since they used to affirm that goodness, kinship ties, and the chastity which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded were true and right. End of quotation.

As for his statement that *qalīlan* is governed by a hidden verb indicated by *tu'minūn*, this is not correct, because that indicating verb (*tu'minūn*) must be either with *mā* as a negative or as a verbal particle, as he claimed. If *mā* is negative, then the hidden verb indicated by *tu'minūn* becomes negated by *mā*, so the sense would be: "You do not believe a little, you do not believe," and a verb negated by *mā* cannot be omitted, nor can what cannot be omitted be omitted, as in *mā aḍrabahu* (how I strike him) being taken as *mā aḍraba Zaydan mā aḍrabahu* (how I strike Zayd, how I strike him). If *mā* is a verbal particle, then *mā* is in the nominative position as the subject of *qalīlan*, meaning: "Your faith is little." Then *qalīlan* has nothing preceding it on which it relies to operate, and it has no governing word. Or *mā* is in the nominative position as the subject, so it would be a subject with no predicate, because what precedes it is accusative, not nominative.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Smallness (*qillah*) is in the sense of non-existence, meaning: you do not believe and you do not take heed at all, and the meaning is: how disbelieving you are and how heedless you are." End of quotation. Here *qalīlan* does not mean pure negation, as he claimed, because that would only occur with *aqalla* (the comparative of "few") as in: "The least man who says that is Zayd," or with *qalla*, as in: "Few men say that except Zayd." It may be used for *qalīlun* and *qalīlatun* when they are in the nominative, as in what they permitted in the line of poetry:

*Few are the voices in it except its bellowing.*

But when it is accusative, as in *qalīlan ḍarabtu* (I struck little) or *qalīlan mā ḍarabtu* (I did not strike little, with *mā* as a verbal particle), this is not permitted. As for *qalīlan mā ḍarabtu*, with *mā* as a verbal particle, it requires *qalīlun* to be nominative, because the verbal particle *mā* is in the nominative position as the subject.

Al-Jahdari and al-Hasan recited *yu'minūn* and *yadhdhakkarūn* with the third person (ya) in both. The remaining seven readers recited with the second person (ta). Ubayy recited with two yā's. The majority recited *tanzīlun* (revelation) with a nominative *ḍamma* (ending *-un*). Abu al-Sammal recited *tanzīlan* with a fatḥah (ending *-an*). The majority recited ﴿wa-law taqawwala﴾ (if he had fabricated). *Taqawwul* means that a person attributes to another a saying that he did not say. Dhakwan and his son Muhammad recited *yaqūlu*, the imperfect of *qāla* (he said), but this reading is contradicted by what the majority's reading clearly expresses. It was also read *wa-law tuquwwila* in the passive voice, with the agent omitted and the object taking its place, which is *baʿḍa* (some) if it was read in the nominative, and if it was read in the accusative with *ʿalaynā* (against Us) it takes the place of the agent. The meaning is: "If someone fabricated against Us." The pronoun in *taqawwala* cannot refer to the Messenger (ﷺ), because such a thing is impossible from him; we deny that this is meant as a supposition regarding him, peace and blessings be upon him.

*Al-aqāwīl* is the plural of a plural, like *bayt*, *abyāt*, and *abāyīt*. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He called the transmitted sayings *aqāwīl* as a diminutive and a belittling, as when you say *al-aʿājīb* and *al-aḍāḥīk*, as if it were the plural of *ufʿūlah* from *qawl*." The apparent meaning of ﴿bi-l-yamīn﴾ (by the right hand) is the limb itself. Al-Hasan said: the meaning is "We cut it off as an example and a punishment," and the *bāʾ* in this case is additional. It has also been said that the seizing is in its literal sense. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The meaning is: if a claimant attributed to Us something We did not say, We would kill him by execution, as kings do with one who lies about them, hastening with wrath and vengeance. He depicted execution in its form so that it would be more terrifying, namely that he is seized by the hand and his neck is struck. The right hand was specified rather than the left because the killer, if he wants to strike the back of the neck, takes hold with his left hand; and if he wants to strike the neck and cut it with the sword, which is more painful for the one being executed because he sees the sword, he takes hold with his right hand."

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "By the right hand" means "by power"; the meaning is that We would have inflicted His punishment upon him with power from Us. Mujahid said: "By might." Al-Suddi said: "We would have punished him with truth," and the *min* in *ʿalā hādhā* is then a particle of connection. Nifṭawayh said: "We would have restrained his right hand from acting." It has also been said: "We would have taken away his strength." It has also been said: "We would have humiliated him and rendered him powerless."

﴿Then We would have cut off his aorta﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is the sinew of the heart. Mujahid said: it is the cord of the heart that is in the back, which is the spinal marrow. The one whose aorta is cut is *mawtūn*. The meaning is: if he fabricated against Us, We would have quickly taken his life.

The pronoun in *ʿanhu* (from him) apparently refers to the one who fabricated. It may also refer to the killing, meaning: none of you could prevent him from that or repel it from him. ﴿And indeed it is a reminder﴾, that is: and indeed the Qur'an, or the Messenger (ﷺ), is a reminder for the God-fearing.

﴿And indeed We know that among you are deniers﴾: this is a threat, meaning: deniers of the Qur'an or of the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿And indeed it is a cause of regret﴾, that is: the Qur'an, from the standpoint that they disbelieved in it, and they see those who believed in it enjoying blessings while they are punished. Muqatil said: their denial of the Qur'an is a cause of regret for them. The pronoun refers to the verbal noun understood from *mukadhdhibīn* (deniers), as in the line of poetry:

*When the fool forbids, he is drawn to it.*

That is, to foolishness. ﴿And indeed it﴾, that is: the Qur'an ﴿is the sure truth﴾. ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾. The discussion of the annexation of *ḥaqq* (truth) to *yaqīn* (certainty) has already been given at the end of al-Waqi'ah.

﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ ﴿and what you do not see﴾ ﴿that it is indeed the word of a noble messenger﴾ ﴿and it is not the word of a poet—little do you believe﴾ ﴿nor the word of a soothsayer—little do you take heed﴾ ﴿it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿and if he had fabricated against Us some sayings﴾ ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ ﴿then We would have cut off his aorta﴾ ﴿and none of you could have held Us back from him﴾ ﴿and indeed it is a reminder for the God-fearing﴾ ﴿and indeed We know that among you are deniers﴾ ﴿and indeed it is a cause of regret for the disbelievers﴾ ﴿and indeed it is the sure truth﴾ ﴿so glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾.

It has also been said that *lā* here is a negation of the oath, meaning: there is no need for an oath in this matter because the truth in it is clear. On this view, its answer is the answer of the oath.
